chunks.content: Introduction Acute aortic syndrome (AAS) is a life-threatening and severe cardiovascular disorder. The prevalence among the population is approximately 2% to 8%, and the incidence is higher in males. The age of onset is mostly between 50 and 70 years . AAS includes aortic dissection (AD), intra-mural hematoma (IMH), and penetrating aortic ulcer (PAU), with AD being the most common. It is caused by various factors that lead to tearing of the aortic intima, with blood flowing into the arterial wall, causing the aortic wall to separate and stratify. The vascular lumen is divided into true and false lumens by the free intimal flap , . The progression of AD is rapid, and mortality is high. The hourly mortality rate within 24 h of onset of symptoms is 2.6%, and in extremely high-risk populations, the mortality rate within two days can be as high as 70% , . Therefore, an early, rapid, and accurate diagnosis of AAS is crucial to reduce mortality. In 1970, Daily et al. proposed the Stanford classification: Types A involves the ascending aorta, while Type B involves the descending thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian artery , . For patients with acute Stanford Type A AD, surgical repair remains the preferred treatment, whereas for patients with Stanford Type B AD, drug therapy is usually applied to control blood pressure and heart rate . For patients suspected of having AD, 5% to 25% have IMH, and in Asia, it is approximately to 30% to 40%. For patients with IMH, 16% to 47% will progress to AD , . PAU accounts for approximately 2% to 7% of patients with AAS and it may progress to IMH, AD, pseudoaneurysm, or aortic rupture, and the risk of rupture is as high as 40% , . Severe sudden chest or back pain is the most common symptom of AD. However, symptoms vary greatly among patients, with many reporting non-specific symptoms and some experiencing no discomfort. Additionally, the results of physical examinations are usually relatively normal. These characteristics make the diagnosis of AD very difficult . Relevant studies have shown that the misdiagnosis rate of AD is 33.8%, indicating that approximately one-third of patients face a higher risk of death solely because of misdiagnosis . Therefore, timely and accurate diagnosis and classification are more conducive to enabling individualized treatment and mortality reduction. With advances in science and technology, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in medical image classification studies has become increasingly widespread – . As early as 1995, investigators began applying convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to the analysis of images . Recently, Hata et al. investigated the diagnostic performance of deep-learning algorithms, based on ordinary computed tomography (CT) images, for AD , and Lee et al. used the Resnet 18 model to detect acute AD, based on chest X-ray films . The gold standard for imaging examination in diagnosing AAS is CT angiography (CTA). Relevant serological indicators such as the D-dimer level are also important auxiliary diagnostic indicators for AAS , . At present, the AI diagnosis research of AAS shows the feature of "strong imaging, weak integration". There are mainly three clinical and technical bottlenecks. Firstly, the clinical incompleteness of single-modal diagnosis. Mainstream research overly relies on single-image analysis, which can identify vascular morphological changes but fails to integrate key clinical evidence such as D-dimer and inflammatory markers. This “information silo” model is contrary to the multi-dimensional comprehensive interpretation thinking of "imaging—laboratory tests—medical history" in clinical practice. It leads to a significantly increased risk of missed diagnosis when there are artifacts, early-stage lesions, or atypical manifestations. Secondly, the shallow processing and insufficient handling of heterogeneity in multimodal fusion are issues. A few studies that have attempted to integrate imaging and clinical data mostly adopt simple concatenation or early fusion strategies, failing to achieve deep semantic alignment across modalities . Clinical indicators and imaging features have significant heterogeneity in terms of data distribution, dimensionality, and semantics. Traditional fusion methods struggle to capture their intrinsic correlations and may even introduce noise . More importantly, the current framework lacks the modeling of complex interaction relationships among clinical indicators (such as the synergistic effect between D-dimer and cytokine storm), which restricts the discriminative power and interpretability of the model. Finally, there is a lack of an AI architecture that conforms to clinical diagnostic reasoning. Clinicians construct associative network linking "imaging abnormalities—physiological disorders—pathological classification". However, most current AI models produce “black box” predictions without explicit diagnostic logic. It difficult for doctors to understand the basis of AI decisions and hindering their trust in such models in the high-pressure environment of emergency care , . In response to the aforementioned bottlenecks, this study proposes a multimodal multi-scale fusion graph neural network (MMMF) with three key innovations:1. By using GNN to implement message passing, biochemical evidence such as abnormal elevation of D-dimer can combine with the subtle changes in the aortic wall in the images, breaking through the traditional information piling-up mode and achieving decision-level fusion. 2. Multi-scale visual coding strategy (solving the problem of early lesion identification). A dual-branch Vision Transformer is introduced to simultaneously extract features at two scales: 32 × 32 (global vascular morphology) and 14 × 14 (local intimal tear and intramural hematoma details). This design mimics the radiologist’s reading habit of "first the whole then the part", balancing the ability to distinguish macroscopic classification and capture microscopic lesions. 3. Clinical interpretability and low-confidence case marking function (addressing the black box trust crisis). The model can proactively identify ambiguous cases in easily confused subgroups such as Group A and Group B, alerting doctors to focus on re-examination, and establishing a new human–machine collaborative model of "AI initial screening—human precise judgment", rather than replacing doctors’ decisions. We collected aortic CTA images and concurrent blood indicators (D-dimer and inflammatory factors) from 493 patients to develop and validate MMMF model. By integrating CTA image features and clinical indicators through a graph neural network to explore the potential of cross-modal fusion in the diagnosis of AAS. We aim to provide a more reliable auxiliary diagnostic tool that reduces misdiagnosis rates and optimize AAS diagnostic workflows. Method Preparation of dataset In strict accordance with the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the imaging data, blood indicators and baseline data of AAS patients and non-AAS patients who underwent CTA examination and blood tests at Dalian Medical University (Dalian, China) from 2019 to 2024 were collected. The collected images were quality controlled by an experienced physician. In total, 986 CTA images were collected (236 in the non-AAS group, 216 in the Stanford Type A AD group, 264 in the Stanford Type B AD group, and 270 in the atypical AD group). This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Dalian Medical University, Dalian, China (Approval Number: PJ-KS-KY-2025–887). Written informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in this retrospective study. Collected CTA images Inclusion criteria Collect the images of AAS patients (n = 375) and non-AAS patients (n = 118) who underwent CTA examination at Dalian Medical University from 2019 to 2024. The images were expected to clearly display the structures of the ascending aorta, descending aorta, and heart, and that the Stanford classification could be performed. Exclusion criteria: Images with poor quality, such as artifacts/insufficient visibility of the ascending aorta. Grouping According to the Stanford classification criteria, patients with AD involving the ascending aorta were assigned to the Stanford Type A group (n = 108); those with AD involving the thoracic descending aorta and its distal segment were assigned to the Stanford Type B group (n = 132); and those with IMH and PAU (n = 135) were assigned to the atypical group. Patients without AD were assigned to the control group (n = 118). Baseline data General information includes Age, sex, hypertension, smoking, coronary heart disease, and coronary CTA stenosis > 50%. Serological indicators included The D-dimer level (mg/L), neutrophil count (× 10 9 /L), lymphocyte count (× 10 9 /L), monocyte count (× 10 9 /L), platelet count(× 10 9 /L), albumin level (g/L), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR), neutrophil-to-platelet ratio (NPR), platelet-to-albumin ratio (PAR), systemic inflammatory response index (SIRI), and systemic immune response index (SII). By performing comparative experiments with different structures, the effects of the different graph-modeling methods on the multi-modal fusion effect were evaluated. Logistic regression analysis was used to explore the indicators related to the occurrence of AAS. P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Among the three groups of AAS patients, the overall degree of coronary artery stenosis is relatively mild; however, a significant proportion (46.9%) have a history of smoking, which may be related to the higher proportion of male patients among AAS patients. The age of AAS patients is mostly concentrated between 50 and 70 years old. The median age of onset for Stanford type A, Stanford type B and atypical groups is 59, 58 and 67 years old respectively. Overall experimental results Table presents the overall experimental results. The proposed MMMF model was compared with a single-modal model, and with other state-of-the-art multi-modal fusion methods, including MBT and VLC-BERT , and the recently developed models with medical image processing capabilities, such as Med-MLLM , , LLaVA-Med and LLaMA4 . For these models, the MLLM was frozen and responses were generated using multi-source input embeddings generated by the corresponding frozen encoder. Similarly, this design was adopted and LLM was used for category prediction. This method involves fine-tuning a classification head for each subtype on top of the LLM, and performing LORA fine-tuning on the LLM. The classification performance was evaluated based on four dimensions: mean accuracy, precision, recall, and F1. This result indicates that the main separability of this task still stems from the imaging modality; the ViT system as a whole outperforms the clinical single-modal approach, and ViT-L/14 is the best visual model, which is in accordance with the benefits of a larger capacity and finer-grained representation. The clinical side (Random Forest/ Fully Connection/ Transformer Small) had an overall significantly low performance, suggesting that noise, such as sparse and missing structured features, and inconsistent dimensions, limited the discriminative power. The key reason why the proposed MMMF model benefits from incorporating clinical data lies in how these data are integrated, rather than their independent discriminative strength. First, clinical features are not directly concatenated or equally weighted with image features. In the new multi-modal baseline, the accuracy of MBT and VLC-BERT were < 0.7, and the precision was also relatively low (weaker than recall), indicating insufficient robustness in cross-modal alignment and fusion. There were possible issues, such as feature redundancy, modality imbalance, or unstable attention distribution; however, VLC-BERT was slightly better than MBT, suggesting that there was a slight improvement in semantic alignment capability. In comparison, LLaVA-Med and LLaMA4 achieved significant improvements in visual language modeling and domain pre-training due to their stronger capabilities; however, they were inferior to MMMF. Moreover, the MLLM model is larger in scale, resulting in additional computational costs. MMMF was simultaneously optimal for all classification metrics, indicating that graph-based relationship modeling effectively achieves true complementary gains rather than merely adjusting the thresholds. The synchronous improvement in precision and recall, and the resulting higher F1, further demonstrate that the decision boundary is more robust and generalizable. Overall, the results simultaneously reveal the bottleneck of single clinical modalities, the fragility of simple multi-modal alignment, and the decisive advantage of relationship-aware fusion in medical multi-modal diagnosis. All baseline models, including MBT and VLC-BERT, were carefully implemented following their original designs and were trained under the same data split, evaluation protocol, and optimization settings as other models. Specifically, both models were fine-tuned on our dataset using supervised classification objectives, rather than evaluated in a zero-shot manner. Therefore, the observed performance gap is not due to insufficient fine-tuning or mismatched training conditions. MBT and VLC-BERT are designed primarily for vision–language or vision–text tasks, where the auxiliary modality is unstructured, high-dimensional, and semantically aligned with visual content (e.g., captions, questions, or commonsense text). In contrast, the “non-visual” modality in our task consists of low-dimensional, heterogeneous, and highly structured clinical indicators (e.g., D-dimer, inflammatory indices), whose semantics are not naturally aligned with visual tokens. Directly applying generic cross-modal attention mechanisms in this scenario can introduce modality noise rather than complementary information, as the models are forced to attend between fundamentally mismatched representations. This often leads to unstable attention weights and suboptimal feature fusion, which has been observed in prior multimodal medical studies. Our results indicate that the primary discriminative signal for AAS classification resides in the CTA imaging modality. Strong vision encoders (e.g., ViT-L/14) already capture most of the separable structure. When generic multimodal fusion is applied without explicitly modeling medical relationships, the additional modality may dilute rather than enhance the decision boundary, explaining why MBT and VLC-BERT do not outperform vision-only baselines. This is consistent with the scenario where there were more misclassifications in the Stanford Type A group in the previous confusion matrix. Overall, the model performed exceptionally well at the macro level, particularly demonstrating high sensitivity and specificity in distinguishing between normal and typical abnormal groups. However, there is still room for improvement in its ability to discriminate between sub-groups with weak phenotypic features and ambiguous boundaries, particularly for the Stanford Type A group. Ablation results The details of the ablation results are presented in Table . From this set of ablation results, it is evident that the performance of the model is mainly influenced by two key factors: the graph structure modeling method (GraphFormer / GAT / GCN) and the resolution of the visual encoder (32 × 32, 14 × 14, dual encoder combination). The overall trend is consistent: GraphFormer consistently outperformed GAT and GCN, and the fusion strategy of the dual encoder significantly outperformed the single-scale input of the visual features. Specifically, the combination of GraphFormer and the dual encoder had the highest accuracy (0.7526), precision (0.7645), recall (0.7526), and F1 (0.7487), indicating that the transformer architecture demonstrated the most significant advantage in multi-modal graph relationship modeling. GraphFormer can capture more distant dependencies between nodes. It achieves global aggregation of cross-modal features in the graph through a self-attention mechanism, enabling the model to have stronger generalization when identifying complex patterns of interaction. In contrast, the performances of GAT and GCN were slightly lower. GAT enhanced the local neighborhood weighting ability through the attention mechanism, thus it was slightly superior to GCN, overall. However, the local aggregation feature limits the capture of long-range dependencies across modalities, resulting in lower global discriminative power than that of GraphFormer. From the perspective of the encoder, the dual encoder (32 × 32 + 14 × 14) consistently outperformed the single scale. The 32 × 32 features were relatively global and suitable for semantic modeling, whereas the 14 × 14 features captured more local details. After their fusion, the model can not only form a robust understanding of the macroscopic anatomical structure but also enable detailed discrimination of the areas of microscopic lesions. This hierarchical feature fusion significantly improves the multi-modal alignment effect and completeness of cross-level information expression. By comparison, the model using only a 32 × 32 encoder had the lowest performance, indicating that it is difficult to achieve stable discrimination of simple fine-grained features without high-level semantics. These ablation results fully validates two points: First, the global relationship modeling of the graph structure

This hierarchical feature fusion significantly improves the multi-modal alignment effect and completeness of cross-level information expression. By comparison, the model using only a 32 × 32 encoder had the lowest performance, indicating that it is difficult to achieve stable discrimination of simple fine-grained features without high-level semantics. These ablation results fully validates two points: First, the global relationship modeling of the graph structure (GraphFormer) is a key mechanism for achieving deep fusion between modalities. Second, multi-scale visual encoding (dual encoder) can significantly enhance the ability of the model to perceive lesion semantics and spatial hierarchy. The combination of the two enabled the MMMF model (GraphFormer) to achieve the best results for all metrics, proving that this design has greater robustness and interpretability in multi-modal medical diagnosis tasks. Discussion With advances in science and technology, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the medical field has become increasingly widespread. Through image analysis, the application of AI has demonstrated excellent performance in the diagnosis and classification of AD. The current AI diagnostic models for acute aortic syndrome (AAS) are facing fundamental bottlenecks in clinical translation: models based on a single imaging modality (such as radiomics and U-Net ) have insufficient specificity, high misdiagnosis rates, and poor generalization due to the lack of integration of key pathophysiological clinical indicators (such as D-dimer). While emerging general-purpose multimodal medical large models (such as LLaVA-Med ) can handle both images and text, their non-customized architectures and large computational costs cannot meet the precise, efficient, and interpretable causal reasoning requirements of the AAS emergency scene. The core gap lies in the fact that there is currently a lack of AI architectures capable of explicitly modeling the medical logical relationships among "physiological indicators—imaging features—clinical classification". This study focuses on the comprehensive analysis of CTA images combined with clinical indicators for the diagnosis of AAS. We propose a multimodal and multiscale fusion model (MMMF). By using Graph Neural Network (GNN), the cross-modal features of CTA images and clinical indicators (such as D-dimer and inflammatory factors) are integrated, thereby enhancing the accuracy of AAS diagnosis and classification. The GNN is not used merely to encode adjacency, but to enable iterative, learnable message passing between image nodes and clinical nodes. Thus, even under a simple topology, the GNN serves as a structured reasoning module, rather than a mere fusion operator. Our experiments already include strong non-graph multimodal fusion methods that rely on attention-based alignment rather than graph reasoning, including: MBT (Attention Bottleneck Transformer) VLC-BERT Large multimodal models such as LLaVA-Med and LLaMA4 (with frozen encoders and task-specific heads). As shown in Table , these non-graph-based fusion approaches consistently underperform the proposed MMMF model across Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1. In contrast, MMMF achieves the best overall performance, indicating that graph-based relational modeling provides additional benefit beyond attention-based fusion alone. MBT and VLC-BERT serve as non-graph, attention-based fusion baselines. Our current graph construction connects clinical indicator nodes exclusively to image nodes, resulting in a bipartite (star-like) topology. This design is motivated by both clinical reasoning principles and modeling considerations: (1) Clinical motivation: preserving the causal role of clinical indicators In the context of acute aortic syndrome (AAS), clinical indicators (e.g., D-dimer, inflammatory indices) are not interpreted in isolation, nor primarily in relation to each other, but rather as physiological responses to underlying structural abnormalities visible on CTA imaging. From a clinical perspective, correlations among laboratory indicators (e.g., between NLR and SIRI) are often secondary manifestations of the same pathological process, rather than independent diagnostic evidence. Directly modeling dense edges among clinical indicators risks amplifying redundant inflammatory signals and may obscure their intended role as auxiliary evidence supporting image-based morphological findings. Therefore, our graph structure reflects a clinically faithful diagnostic logic: clinical indicators serve to contextualize and validate imaging findings, rather than forming an independent reasoning subgraph. (2) Modeling motivation: avoiding redundancy and instability under limited sample size Many clinical indicators used in this study are mathematically or biologically correlated (e.g., NLR, PLR, SII, SIRI). Explicitly introducing edges among these nodes would create a densely connected clinical subgraph, which in our preliminary experiments led to: over-smoothing of clinical node representations, reduced interpretability of message passing, and unstable training due to multicollinearity, especially given the moderate cohort size. By restricting clinical nodes to interact only with image nodes, the GNN is encouraged to learn cross-modal relevance (i.e., which clinical indicators are informative for which imaging patterns), rather than rediscovering known correlations among laboratory variables. (3) Empirical support from ablation results: Our ablation experiments demonstrate that even under this constrained topology, the proposed MMMF model consistently outperforms: image-only baselines, clinical-only baselines, and alternative multimodal fusion approaches. Thus, it has clear prospects for clinical application. First, it effectively resolves the clinical challenges associated with rapid and accurate triage. As AAS can be fatal, the success rate of treatment is highly dependent on the time from patient presentation to diagnosis. The model is capable of simultaneously processing CTA images and key clinical indicators, such as the D-dimer level, enabling it to achieve rapid and automated preliminary screening and classification of “normal”, “typical dissection” and “atypical dissection”. The high recognition ability for the control and atypical dissection groups, enables it to serve as an efficient “screening filter”, liberating physicians from heavy initial screening, and allowing them to prioritize high-risk or complex cases marked by the model. This significantly shortens the initial screening diagnosis and treatment path, thereby winning precious time for rescue. Second, this model is dedicated to reducing the rate of missed and misdiagnosed AAS, particularly atypical dissection, and to improving the rate of early identification. Simple image analysis may overlook early, and subtle lesion features, due to artifacts, image quality, or insufficient physician experience, whereas a single D-dimer level, although highly sensitive, has insufficient specificity. The deep cross-modal interaction implemented by the MMMF model using a GNN, essentially enables a combination between the morphological evidence in the images and the physiological and biochemical indices of the patients, mutually corroborating and complementing each other. In clinical deployment, this feature can be transformed into an advantage; the system can proactively identify and flag “low confidence” cases, prompting senior physicians to conduct a joint consultation or suggest a short-term imaging follow-up. This promotes the establishment of a human–machine collaborative diagnosis and treatment system, where AI-derived tools efficiently process a large amount of routine information and identify potential risks. On the other hand, physicians focus on the final, complex clinical decisions, converting the “uncertainty” output from the AI-derived tools into an opportunity to deepen diagnostic thinking, ultimately achieving the optimal allocation of medical resources and an overall improvement in the accuracy of diagnosis and of treatment. This study has several limitations that warrant discussion. First, the dataset of this study was quality-controlled by a single doctor, which might have introduced certain subjective biases. Future studies should involve multiple independent reviewers with inter-observer reliability assessment to mitigate this. Second, the data were obtained from a single-center with limited generalizability and were retrospective, thereby lacking multi-center validation. Third, the model has not been evaluated in a prospective clinical trial to determine the effect on patient prognosis. Integrating AI-derived tools into clinical workflows is highly challenging, and their diagnostic performance may be limited by the equipment and operator proficiency in different hospitals. To overcome these limitations, in future studies, multi-center data should be included, prospective validation performed, and the adaptability of the model should be explored in different clinical settings. Conclusions An MMMF model, based on a GNN, has been constructed to enable the precise diagnosis and classification of AAS. The model achieves effective complementarity and decision-level fusion of cross-modal information by deeply integrating CTA imaging features with clinical indicators such as the D-dimer level. The comprehensive diagnostic performance is significantly superior to that of single-modal and other mainstream multi-modal methods. The model has demonstrated significant potential for clinical application. On the one hand, it can serve as an efficient screening tool to rapidly distinguish normal from typical cases, significantly reducing the workload of physicians. Moreover, it can intelligently identify the “grey areas” in diagnosis, marking cases with a low confidence level to guide focused clinical re-examination, providing an effective solution for building a new model of human–machine collaborative diagnosis. In future, it will be necessary to conduct multi-center prospective studies to further verify the generalizability of the model and to promote deep integration with clinical workflows.

Background Low back pain (LBP) is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide, with peak disability burden found in the 80- to 84-year age group [ ]. In 2017, the age-specific point prevalence of LBP in older adults ranged between 14.7% in males aged 65- to 69-years to 22.7% in females aged 80- to 89-years [ , ]. Among older adults, 60% have LBP-related functional disability, which substantially limits their ability to engage in activities of daily living and reduces mobility [ , ]. Diagnostic imaging is commonly used in the management of LBP, with approximately one-quarter of people who present to primary care with LBP referred for imaging [ ]. Imaging is recommended to rule out underlying serious pathology (e.g., tumour, infection, fracture), or recommended when surgical management is considered [ – ]. Current estimates of the frequency of imaging commonly exclude older adult populations. In a previous review of imaging use for LBP [ ], only two of the 45 included studies assessed the proportion of older adults referred for imaging [ , ], with proportions of imaging in the first four weeks varying between 28.8% [ ] and 38.3% [ ]. Clinical practice guidelines recommend that imaging for LBP is primarily indicated if there are signs or symptoms of possible underlying pathology, or ‘red flags’, or where there is a lack of improvement in the presenting condition after four to six weeks of appropriate management [ , , ]. Early imaging in older adults without suspected underlying pathology has been associated with poorer outcomes and increased downstream healthcare use [ , ]. In older guidelines, age over 50 by itself was considered a red flag for possible serious pathology [ , ]; however, more recent recommendations consider older age within a group of risk factors for fracture and not a red flag by itself [ , ]. Variability in imaging use in older adults is high, potentially indicating clinician uncertainty of when imaging is needed. For example, in one study, individual clinicians referred between 6% and 54% of older adults with LBP for imaging [ ]. In chiropractic practice, one in seven adult patients are over 65 years of age and of these patients, nearly 56% present with a back problem [ ]. Controversy related to the appropriate use of diagnostic imaging for LBP practice has been reported in chiropractic practice [ ]. In contrast to LBP clinical guideline recommendations, some chiropractors report using imaging routinely to assess for contraindications to spinal manipulation or perform biomechanical analysis [ ]. High velocity low amplitude (HVLA) manipulation is the most common form of treatment to be performed by chiropractors, but it is selected as a treatment less often in older patients [ ]. HVLA manipulation is used in only 60% of chiropractic encounters with patients aged 65 years or over, compared to 92% of encounters with younger patients [ ], possibly reflecting a perceived increased risk of harm due to an underlying pathology, with conditions such as osteoporosis (and related fractures) and tumours more likely to occur in older adult populations [ , ]. Arguments have been made, therefore, that intention to use HVLA manipulation may increase the need for diagnostic imaging to assess for underlying pathology that would contraindicate manipulation [ ]. Previous studies in cohorts of chiropractic patients have found relatively low incidence of serious pathology or anomalies that would be likely to contraindicate manual therapy [ , – ]; however, these studies did not specifically assess older adults. The overall aim of this study was to assess the use of imaging in older adults with a new episode of LBP who sought chiropractic care and to describe the types of radiographic findings. The specific aims were to: (i) determine the proportion of older adults with LBP presenting for chiropractic care who reported receiving low back imaging across the 12-month follow-up period and describe the type and timing of imaging received; (ii) describe participant characteristics associated with receiving imaging; and. (iii) describe the types of imaging findings in older adults receiving imaging of the low back. All participants meeting inclusion criteria and consenting to participate in the BACE: C-A study were included in the current analysis. Follow-up questionnaires were completed at two- and six-weeks and three-, six-, nine-, and 12-months. Data analysis The proportion of participants who received imaging was reported as: (i) the proportion reporting receiving at least one type of imaging across the 12-month period; (ii) the proportion receiving at least one type of imaging at each of the questionnaire timepoints; (iii) the proportion receiving each imaging type (x-ray, CT, MRI, other) across the 12-month period and at each time point; and (iv) the proportion reporting their first imaging across the 12-month study period at each time point. Proportions were presented descriptively as a percentage with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). Participant characteristics were reported descriptively using means and standard deviations for continuous variables (age, pain intensity, disability) and proportions with 95% CIs for categorical variables (gender, duration of back pain, previous episode of back pain, previous health care, possible serious cause of LBP, history of cancer, taking glucocorticoid medication, imaging beliefs). Discussion In a cohort of 217 people aged ≥ 55 years who sought chiropractic care for a new episode of LBP, 132 (60.8%) reported receiving diagnostic imaging either prior to their first consult with the chiropractor or within the 12-month follow-up period. Approximately two-thirds (68.2%) of participants were referred for imaging by a chiropractor. X-rays (44.7%) were the most common imaging modality received, followed by CT (30.8%) and MRI (13.8%), with the majority receiving between one and two different forms of imaging. Participants who received imaging tended to have higher low back disability, more previous healthcare use for LBP, more frequent pain extending below the knee, more suspected serious pathology, and beliefs that imaging is necessary for the management of LBP. Degenerative change was the most common imaging finding reported, present in 94.8% of participants who provided imaging reports. All participants who received a CT scan or MRI had degenerative change (disc and/or facet) and one or more disc lesions (disc bulge, herniation, or annular tear/fissure). 15% of people providing imaging reports had underlying pathology or trauma of likely clinical significance, including osteopenia/possible osteoporosis or benign bone tumours. No conditions requiring immediate or urgent medical referral, such as infection, cancer, or new traumatic fractures were identified. This is comparable to the present study where 23.7% of participants received imaging prior to or at their first consult with the chiropractor, and by six weeks 31.8% had received imaging. Results are also comparable to a meta-analysis of 8 studies in primary care (medical, chiropractic, physiotherapy, osteopathy), which found the proportion of low back imaging in adults of any age presenting for care to be 24.8% (95%CI: 19.3-31.1%) [ ]. In the current study, we found that an additional 22.6% of participants received their first diagnostic imaging between three and six months; however, this was not seen in a previous study of older adults presenting for medical care where total imaging only increased from 28.8 to 32.2% (increase of 3.4%) between one to six months [ ]. Increased imaging after three months in our study may reflect guideline recommendations for ‘watchful waiting’ [ ] or a trial of care [ ], or the reassessment of persistent or recurrent LBP. However, the reasons for imaging use, and whether they aligned with guideline recommendations for each participant, were not assessed in this study. The characteristics of those who received imaging were broadly consistent with clinical practice guideline recommendations, including suspected underlying pathology and leg pain extending below the knee [ – ]. Participant beliefs about the importance or necessity of imaging have previously been shown to be a potential driver of increased imaging use [ ], consistent with the results of this study. However, the proportion of participants agreeing that imaging is necessary to assess LBP was higher in this study (61.0%) compared to previous studies, performed in chiropractic and medical settings, ranging between 41.5% and 54.3% [ , ]. Older age in a general adult population of people presenting for medical care has been associated with increased beliefs in the importance of imaging for LBP and may explain the higher proportion of people believing that imaging was needed seen in this study [ ]. The types of imaging findings observed in this study are generally consistent with previous literature. Degenerative changes in the lumbar spine, seen in nearly all participants providing imaging reports, are well recognised to be frequently observed on diagnostic imaging, especially as people age [ ], and to be more common in people with LBP [ , ]. Previous studies have only assessed the types of imaging findings in adults of any age, including findings on lumbar radiographs in chiropractic settings [ , , ] and findings on MRI in medical settings [ , , , ]. The current study found higher proportions of spondylolisthesis and spinal stenosis, possibly due to an increase in these conditions with older age [ ]. In contrast, while low proportions have been reported in previous studies [ , , ], no recent fractures, cancer, or spinal infections were identified. The potential to detect serious pathology was limited in this study by the exclusion of people with a diagnosis of serious pathology or contraindications to chiropractic care at baseline from the BACE: C-A cohort and the low number of imaging reports assessed. The exclusion criteria reflect clinical practice in that people diagnosed with serious pathology or contraindications that are outside the scope of chiropractic care at initial assessment would likely be referred directly for medical management [ ]. People presenting for medical care also tend to have poorer general health than people presenting for chiropractic care [ ]; it is likely that people in poorer health, and more likely to have serious pathology, would self-select to present to medical rather than chiropractic care for assessment. We specifically included outcome measures to capture imaging data across the 12-month study period and provide detailed data on the use of imaging in this cohort. Limitations include study exclusion criteria, self-reported data, participant withdrawal, and the number and type of imaging reports received from participants, which impact the generalisability and validity of results. People with a diagnosed pathology (e.g., cancer, infection) or contraindications for chiropractic care were excluded from the study, potentially resulting in an underestimation of imaging use. Categorisation of imaging findings may have been inconsistent due to variations in imaging reporting, potentially impacting the validity of results. Implications for clinical practice and research Nearly all imaging reports assessed had at least one type of degenerative change present; however, clinical relevance is uncertain. Degenerative changes are expected in an older populations, are commonly found in asymptomatic populations [ ], but are also more common in people with LBP [ , ] and have been associated with worse long-term pain and disability [ ]. The presence of degenerative change on imaging does not generally indicate a change in treatment approach, and no specific interventions have been identified as more effective when degenerative changes are present [ ]. Therefore, identifying degenerative changes on imaging has limited impact on patient management. Similarly, disc lesions (including disc bulges and disc herniation) were present on all people who received a CT or MRI. 1. Introduction Multinodular and vacuolating neuronal tumor (MVNT) is a rare, benign neuronal lesion with typical radiological and histological appearance [ , ]. This lesion was first defined approximately a decade ago and was included as a unique architectural pattern in the 2016 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System [ ]. In the updated (2021) Fifth Edition of the WHO classification, it was recognized as a separate entity in the Glioneuronal and Neuronal Tumors group [ ]. MVNTs are usually discovered as an incidental finding on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), but in some cases, they may present with seizures or seizure equivalents [ ]. Histologically they comprise tumor cells with remarkable stromal vacuolization arranged in nodules, mostly located in the temporal and parietal lobes with a predilection for subcortical-juxtacortical areas [ ]. They are generally considered as ‘leave-me-alone’ lesions, showing no interval changes on the follow-up MRIs for years. Therefore, accurate and reliable diagnosis is important for avoiding misdiagnosis and unnecessary intervention. The primary differential diagnosis for MVNTs is dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors (DNETs), another cortically-based benign lesion of glioneuronal-neuronal origin. DNETs are also seizure-related lesions and may have some imaging features that overlap with MVNTs [ , ]. Since MVNTs are rare and most cases have been described recently, there are limited data on their clinical and radiological features in the published literature. Moreover, there are no studies comparing the MRI features of MVNT and DNET lesions [ , , ]. Hence, the aim of this study was to make a comprehensive characterization of the clinical and MRI features of MVNTs, and analyze the radiological differences from DNETs, which stand out as the main differential diagnosis. 2. Informed consent was obtained from each participant included in the study group. 2.2. Patient selection Data of patients with a suspected MRI-based diagnosis of MVNT between January 2018 and December 2022 were collected from the hospital database. In addition, patients diagnosed with DNETs on histopathological examination and who had MRIs in the same time period were included in the study. The DNET lesions were type 1a (cystic-like) and type 1b (polycystic-like) according to the classification introduced by Chassoux et al [ ]. Patients with prior head trauma, who had undergone cranial surgery, had a history of chemotherapy/cranial radiotherapy, a intracranial accompanying mass lesion, a diagnosis of radiological subtype of two or three for DNET lesions, no follow-up MRI examinations or less than one year MRI follow-up for MVNT lesions that did not have histopathological confirmation were excluded from the study. Consequently, 41 patients who met the inclusion criteria were included in the study and categorized into two groups: MVNT (21 patients) and DNET (20 patients). The diagnosis was histopathologically confirmed in three patients in the MVNT group. Demographic data and clinical findings were recorded for each patient. 2.3. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows 23.0 (IBM SPSS Statistics, Armonk, NY, USA). Discussion The clinical and MRI features of MVNT cases were evaluated in detail and compared with those of DNETs, which was the main differential diagnosis. Given the markedly different treatment regimens and prognoses, it is crucial to make a distinction between MVNTs and DNETs. MVNTs are considered benign lesions without any potential for malignancy and evolution unless they cause seizures. Thus, these lesions can be sufficiently managed on follow-up MRIs [ ]. On the other hand, surgical treatment is essential following the diagnosis in DNETs [ ]. The primary imaging modality for the diagnosis of MVNTs is MRI, and these lesions have a distinctive characteristic appearance. MVNTs have lesions with a bubbly appearance located in the deep cortical ribbon and superficial subcortical white matter. They are observed as hyperintense on both T2WI and FLAIR sequences and do not enhance. They also do not show edema or mass effect [ , , ]. Similarly, DNETs are lesions that are hyperintense on T2WI and FLAIR, do not enhance in most cases, and do not cause mass effect [ , , ]. Subtypes 1a and 1b, which were also included in the current study, are defined as cystic/polycystic-like and may have a soap bubble appearance, mimicking MVNTs [ ]. Thus, the overlapping imaging findings can make the differentiation of MVNT and specific DNET subtypes challenging. Therefore, the differential diagnosis of MVNTs and type 1 DNET lesions were focused on in the present study. One of the features that helps to distinguish DNETs from MVNTs is cortical involvement [ , ]. However, cortical involvement has been reported in up to 57% of MVNTs [ ]. In the current study, cortical involvement of MVNTs was found at a rate of 42.8%. Moreover, although DNETs are mainly cortical-based lesions, they also involve the adjacent white matter at varying degrees [ ]. Consistently, extension from the cortex to the subcortical white matter was observed in all of the DNET cases in the present study. This revealed that cortex and white matter involvement may not be reliable in differentiating MVNTs from DNETs in cases with overlapping MRI findings. The FLAIR hyperintense rim sign is a well-known specific appearance in DNETs [ , , , ]. It is also speculated that the presence of this ring on postoperative imaging indicates a residual or recurrent tumor [ ]. In a study by Isler et al. [ ], this was found in four (19%) of the 21 DNET patients. However, Parmar et al. [ ] reported that nine of the 11 DNET patients and two of 21 of those in the non-DNET control group displayed this sign, resulting in a high sensitivity and specificity for DNETs, as 82% and 90% respectively. Herein, it was detected in 8 (40%) of the 20 DNET patients, while no such rim was demonstrated in the MVNT patients, resulting in a sensitivity of 40% and specificity of 100%. DNETs, similar to MVNTs, do not show diffusion restriction, but were reported to have high relative ADC values [ ]. In a study by Daghistani et al. [ ], the relative mean ADC values of two DNET groups were calculated as 2.22 ± 0.59 × 10 −3 and 2.21 ± 0.74 × 10 −3 mm 2 /s. The current results were the similar to those in the literature, as none of the MVNT and DNET lesions showed diffusion restriction. The median relative ADC values for the MVNT and DNET groups herein were 0.99 ± 0.18 × 10 −3 and 1.68 ± 0.34 × 10 −3 mm 2 /s respectively. Furthermore, the DWI intensity of each lesion in the MVNT and DNET groups were also evaluated. Noticeably, in 20 (95%) of the 21 MVNT patients, lesions showed high DWI signal intensity compared with the normal appearance of the white matter without associated hypointensity on the ADC maps. However, none of the DNET lesions showed hyperintensity on DWI. In studies by Lecler et al. [ ] and Nunes et al. [ ], mild high signal intensity on DWI was mentioned for some particular cases. Clinical presentation and lesion location may aid in the differentiation between DNETs and MVNTs. Most of the DNET cases in the published literature presented with drug-resistant epilepsy. On the other hand, MVNTs are often detected incidentally on MRI studies [ , ]. In symptomatic MVNT cases, the most common symptoms are headache and seizures [ , ]. In the present study, the most dominant clinical presentation in the DNET cases was seizure (70%). Similar to the literature, headache (13/21) and seizure (3/21) were the most common symptoms in the MNVT cases. The most common location of DNETs is the temporal lobe (62%), followed by the frontal lobe (31%). On the other hand, in MVNTs, the lesion location is not consistent in different studies [ , ]. Lecler et al. [ ] reported that MVNTs were mostly located in the frontal and parietal lobe. In a study conducted by Huse et al. [ ], the most common location was reported as the temporal lobe. In addition, in some cases, more than one lobe may be affected [ ]. In the current MVNT group, there were similar rates of involvement in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. Moreover, in three cases, more than one lobe was affected. This study had several limitations. First, it was conducted on a limited number of patients and had a retrospective design. Second, the diagnosis was histopathologically confirmed in only three of the patients in the MVNT group in order to provide a persistent seizure-free state. However, no interval changes were observed in the follow-up MRIs of the MVNTs that were not confirmed histopathologically, for at least 12 months. 5. Conclusion MVNT is a rare and stable tumor, which is generally considered as a ‘leave-me-alone’ lesion showing no interval changes on follow-up MRIs. Surgical removal of MVNT is unnecessary unless it is symptomatic. Detailed characterization of its diagnostic and discriminative MRI features, which enables the differentiation from DNET, has substantial importance for the accurate diagnosis and the avoidance of unnecessary surgical interventions.

1 Introduction Traditional Chinese Medicines (TCMs) are a major component of China’s traditional medical technology and culture, and has been the main material means for the Chinese people to prevent and treat diseases for thousands of years. It has the distinctive features of “multi-component, multi-target, multi-pathway and multi-action”, but the pharmacological components of many TCMs are still uncertain. Scientifically and comprehensively controlling and evaluating the quality of TCMs is a key bottleneck and technical difficulty in the modernization of TCMs development. The quality control (QC) methods of TCMs should strive to achieve the technical specifications of exact content, clear structure, and unambiguous efficacy. At present, the active ingredients of TCMs are difficult to be thoroughly elucidated, and the technical level of TCMs quality control is far from the characteristics of the material system of TCMs, all of which make it difficult for the current TCMs quality control and evaluation model to scientifically and comprehensively control and evaluate the quality of TCMs ( ). Nowadays, most commonly used methods for quality evaluation of TCMs are high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) ( ), gas chromatography (GC) ( ) and their combination with mass spectrometry (MS) ( , ), which proved useful in quanlitative and quantitative determination of index components. Nevertheless, problems such as poor correlation between QC indexes and the effectiveness of TCMs, and poor specificity persist, which hinder the modern QC of TCMs. Moreover, TCMs is a synergistic combination of multiple components with poly-pharmacological effects, and the content of a single or several index components can hardly reflect the panorama of TCMs quality ( ). In 2016, Academician Liu Changxiao's team proposed the concept of TCMs quality marker (Q-Marker), which has the basic characteristics of specificity, effectiveness, measurability, and relevance to the TCMs theory; it is a new concept and model for QC of TCMs plants and products, which inspires a new development direction for the TCMs quality, and is important in promoting the modernization and internationalization of TCMs ( , ). In recent years, with the rapid development of modern instrumental analysis technology and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, the quality control and evaluation mode of TCMs is gradually shifting from relying on traditional experience, detection of main active ingredients and index components to multiple index components, “one measurement, multiple evaluation”, fingerprinting, biomarkers, and others. Many new technical means of quality control and evaluation are emerging, and the approaches of discovering Q-Marker of TCMs are gradually changing from active ingredient detection to the flexible applications of network pharmacology ( , ), chemometrics ( , ), molecular docking ( , ) and other means of prediction, as well as fingerprinting ( ) and other methods for corroboration, to name a few. Such methods mostly focused on strategies, and it is difficult to really reach effective corroboration of Q-Markers of TCMs. Mass Spectrometry Imaging (MSI) is a novel technique for visual analysis and detection, which has been recognized as an effective tool for detecting and identifying complex molecules in samples ( , ), and is widely used in numerous fields such as life sciences, biomedicine and environmental toxicology. How to discover and confirm Q-Marker of TCMs is a difficult problem that has not been effectively solved and needs to be studied in depth. These compounds are closely related to the functional properties of TCMs and can be used as markers to reflect the safety and efficacy of TCMs ( ). 2.3 Basic requirements and discovery principles of TCMs Q-marker The TCMs Q-Markers should be: (1) specialized metabolites inherent in TCMs herbs and products, or chemical substances formed during processing and preparation; (2) chemical substances that are solely present in a herb (and/or its TCMs decoction pieces) and not from other herbs; (3) substances with clear chemical structure and biological activity; (4) substances that can be identified qualitatively and quantified; (5) substances that are representative of the “ruler” herbs, e.g., “monarch”, “minister”, and “assistant” herbs, according to the principle of the preferred ”ruler“ herbs in a TCMs formula ( ). The validation of Q-Marker should be based on the ”five principles“ of validity, i.e., specificity, transmission and traceability, measurability, prescription dispensing, and validation of candidate TCMs Q-Markers ( ) ( , , ). 2.3.1 Validity In TCMs, “validity” is the core element of Q-Marker. The understanding of “effectiveness” in the theoretical system of TCMs is based on the “potency” and “efficacy” of drugs, and the change process of the body should also be considered to reach the understanding of “efficacy”, “property” and “process in the body”. The in vivo exposure and pharmacokinetics of TCMs chemical groups are the material basis for the expression of “effectiveness” of TCMs. For example, NHBA, an anti-insomnia candidate isolated from Gastrodia elata Bl. MSI was applied to examine the absorption, distribution, metabolism, elimination (ADME) and pharmacokinetics of candidate TCMs Q-Marker in the body, to clarify the role and distribution of candidate Q-Marker, and to explore the distribution tendency and expression of their biological effects, which is an important basis for confirming the Q-Marker of TCMs. 2.3.2 Specificity At present, there are many medicinal materials in the quality standard of TCMs that take the ubiquitous components (e.g., chlorogenic acid, rutin, etc.) as the content measurement indexes for the QC.
